To: group:levy-longsight-noticeboard
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: Please talk to your kids about the fake pills

Parents and teenagers, please take a minute to read this and share it. The police have put a warning on here about fake blue tablets being sold locally as diazepam or “Xanax”. Some have been found to contain nitazenes, which are synthetic opioids and can be far stronger than heroin. You can’t tell what’s in a pill just by looking at it or by what someone says it is.

If someone has taken something and becomes unwell, ring 999 straight away. Don’t wait to see if they get better, and don’t put them to bed to sleep it off. Tell the call handler what you know and follow their instructions. You don’t need to be certain what they’ve taken before you call.

Signs to look out for include extreme drowsiness, pinpoint pupils (the black bits in the middle of the eyes looking very small), slow or noisy breathing and blue lips. If someone is difficult to wake or their breathing doesn’t sound right, make that call. Put your phone on speaker so you can follow the call handler’s instructions.

I’m an ICU nurse and I know people can panic in an emergency. Sometimes mates think the kindest thing is to put someone in bed, then ring for help hours later when they realise something is badly wrong. By then, their brain may have been without enough oxygen for too long. Please don’t leave them alone and hope they’ll sleep it off.

And please don’t be scared to call because you think you or your mate might get in trouble. The police have said their priority is preserving life. Tell the call handler honestly what you know so the person can get the right help.

Naloxone nasal spray can temporarily reverse an opioid overdose, including one caused by nitazenes. You can get a free kit from Brightpath drug and alcohol service on Stockport Road, next to the launderette. Anyone can ask, no names needed, and training takes about 10 minutes. They’re open Monday to Friday 10–4, and until 7 on Thursdays. If you have naloxone and think someone may have overdosed, use it and ring 999 straight away. It doesn’t replace an ambulance.

I had this chat with my lad last night over his tea. He’s 14, so there were a few eye rolls, but he listened and asked me what pinpoint pupils meant. It doesn’t have to be a big lecture. Just make sure they know what to look for and that they can ring 999 without waiting or worrying about being told off.

Please have that conversation this week, not after half term or whenever you get round to it. And please stop slagging the kids off. Scared kids don’t ring for help, and that’s exactly what we need them to do.

Please share this, not just like it. It might reach someone who needs to know what to do.
